items.zh: 兼治 · 兼轉兼不轉治

zh: 第四、明兼治者，亦出《摩訶衍論》解八念念捨文中。彼論云：「菩薩法施者，法施因緣，或復說法，或現神通，或復放光，如是等利益度脫眾生，名為法施。復次，行法施者，應當善識眾生煩惱多少，或但有一煩惱病，或兩兩雜，或三三雜。若一煩惱，說一法治；兩兩雜者，說二法治；三三雜者，說三法治。」此即是兼治相。一病說一法治，如前說。兩病二法治者，如有貪欲病，復有瞋恚，當用不淨、慈心觀共治。何以故？若但用一法，雖偏治一邊，復增一邊，則為過失。今二法相兼，病則皆差。或不淨兼慈，或慈兼不淨，今應隨病起，以義斟酌。兼三兼四，乃至五等，悉有其義，今不具說。
en: Fourth, clarifying combined treatment: this, too, is given in the Mahāyāna treatise, within its explanation of the passage on the eight recollections' recollection of relinquishment. That treatise says: "As for a bodhisattva's giving of the Dharma: through the causes and conditions of giving the Dharma, one may expound the teaching, or manifest supernormal powers, or emit light — benefiting and liberating sentient beings through such means as these is called giving the Dharma. Furthermore, one who practices giving the Dharma should skillfully recognize how many afflictions a sentient being carries — whether only a single afflictive ailment, or two mixed together, or three mixed together. If there is a single affliction, a single dharma is taught as its treatment; if two are mixed together, two dharmas are taught as their treatment; if three are mixed together, three dharmas are taught as their treatment." This is precisely the mark of combined treatment.

A single ailment treated by a single dharma is as described above. As for two ailments treated by two dharmas together: if a person has both the ailment of craving and the ailment of anger, one should use the contemplation of impurity together with the contemplation of loving-kindness to treat both at once. Why is this? If only a single method were used, although it might treat one side, it would only aggravate the other — this would itself be an error. Here, with the two methods combined together, both ailments are cured at once — whether the contemplation of impurity combined with loving-kindness, or loving-kindness combined with the contemplation of impurity, one should weigh and judge according to whichever ailment has actually arisen. Combining three, combining four, and even combining five methods together, all have their own applicable sense — this is not given here in full.

zh: 第五、明兼不轉治者，此義亦如轉治、不轉治意，但於兼中對病發多少，還約上轉、不轉意細推可見。
en: Fifth, clarifying combined transposed-and-non-transposed treatment: this sense, too, follows the same pattern already given for transposed and non-transposed treatment — only here, among however many ailments have arisen in combination, one applies the same distinction between transposed and non-transposed given above, and this may be seen through careful reflection.

Combined treatment addresses a case the first three antidote types quietly assume away: real practitioners rarely present with a single, isolated ailment. Treating craving and anger together by combining their two matched antidotes, rather than picking one and letting the other fester, is a practical acknowledgment that the fifteen-fold taxonomy is analytic rather than how affliction actually shows up in a given sitting.

items.en: Treatment Through Neither Matching, Transposing, Nor Combining

zh: 第六、非對非轉非兼治者，即是第一義悉檀波若正觀。此觀通能治十五種病，亦通能發十五種門禪，所以言非對非轉非兼治。正觀法性即法，不可以法對法，故云非對正觀，無偏不增，餘病不須轉也。力能遍破眾病，故不須兼。雖不得能破、所破，而治諸不善，悉皆除滅，故名為治。是以《摩訶衍》云：「有三昧但能除貪，不能除瞋，不能除癡，有三昧能除三毒。」即是今所明正觀第一義悉檀也。
en: Sixth, clarifying treatment that is neither matched, transposed, nor combined: this is precisely the right contemplation of prajñā, the siddhānta of ultimate meaning. This contemplation is able, in common, to treat all fifteen ailments, and is able, in common, to bring forth all fifteen gates of dhyāna as well — hence it is said to be neither matched, transposed, nor combined. Right contemplation is itself the very nature of dharmas, itself dharma — one dharma cannot be matched against another dharma, hence it is said to be unmatched. Right contemplation, being without any partial bias, does not aggravate any other ailment, and so needs no transposing; its power is able to break through every ailment universally, and so it has no need to be combined with anything else. Although nothing can be found that breaks through, and nothing that is broken through, every unwholesome dharma is nonetheless treated and utterly removed — hence it is called treatment. Hence the Mahāyāna treatise says: "There is a samādhi able only to remove craving, unable to remove anger or delusion; and there is a samādhi able to remove all three poisons together" — this latter is precisely the right contemplation, the siddhānta of ultimate meaning, clarified here.

zh: 所以波若一觀能治五病者：一、正觀能治貪欲，如《思益經》云：「貪欲之人以淨觀得脫，不以不淨，世尊自知。」二、正觀能治瞋者，如《般若》說：「我昔為歌利王割截身體，爾時無我相、人相、眾生相，則瞋恚不生。」故知實相能治於瞋。三、正觀能破治癡者，智慧破於無明，其義可見，故《涅槃經》云：「明時無闇，闇時無明。有智慧時則無煩惱，有煩惱時則無智慧。」四、正觀能治覺觀者，正觀心中，語言道斷，心行處滅，則覺觀從何而生？故《維摩詰經》言：「云何息攀緣？謂心無所得。」五、正觀能治罪障者，如前引《普賢觀》云：「端坐念實相，是名第一懺。眾罪如霜露，慧日能消除。」
en: As for why the single contemplation of prajñā is able to treat all five ailments: first, right contemplation is able to treat craving — as the Viśeṣacinti Sūtra says: "Those with craving are liberated through the pure contemplation, not through the impure — the World-Honored One knows this of himself." Second, right contemplation is able to treat anger — as the Prajñāpāramitā says: "When, in the past, I had my body cut apart limb by limb by King Kalinga, at that very moment there was no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being — and so no anger arose." Hence it is known that the true mark itself is able to treat anger. Third, right contemplation is able to break through and treat delusion — wisdom breaks through ignorance; the sense of this can be readily seen. Hence the Nirvāṇa Sūtra says: "When there is brightness, there is no darkness; when there is darkness, there is no brightness. When there is wisdom, there is no affliction; when there is affliction, there is no wisdom." Fourth, right contemplation is able to treat discursive thought — within right contemplation's own mind, the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished; from what, then, could discursive thought possibly arise? Hence the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "How does one bring the chasing after objects to rest? By the mind's having nothing at all that it can find." Fifth, right contemplation is able to treat the obstruction of offense — as already cited above from the Samantabhadra Contemplation Sūtra: "Sitting upright and being mindful of the true mark — this is called the foremost repentance. Every offense, like frost or dew, the sun of wisdom is able to dissolve away entirely."

zh: 復次，如世餘藥，各隨對治，能治一病，不能遍治一切病也。阿竭陀藥即能遍治一切眾病，是名非對非轉非兼治，亦能具足一切禪門。如《大品經》說：「欲學一切善法，當學般若。」所以者何？譬如王來，必有營從。若般若慧發，則一心具足萬行。此則可以如意寶珠為喻。
en: Furthermore: it is like every other worldly medicine, each matched to its own particular ailment, able to treat only that one ailment and no other — unable to treat every ailment universally. The agada medicine, however, is able to treat every ailment universally — this is precisely what is meant by treatment that is neither matched, transposed, nor combined, and it is likewise able to be complete in every gate of dhyāna at once. As the Larger Sūtra says: "Wishing to learn every wholesome dharma, one should learn prajñā." Why is this? It is like a king's arrival, which is necessarily accompanied by his whole retinue — once the wisdom of prajñā is brought forth, the whole of the myriad practices is thereby complete within a single mind. This may be illustrated by the simile of the wish-fulfilling jewel.

This sixth and final antidote type is the same move the treatise has made twice before in this fascicle alone — embodying-truth stopping breaking through the other two kinds of stopping, and the vajra wheel completing the other four wheels — a single approach through direct wisdom that supersedes, rather than joins, every graduated technique before it. The agada-medicine simile (a legendary cure-all in classical Indian medicine) makes the point precisely: the fifteen matched antidotes are each a specific medicine for a specific ailment, while prajñā's right contemplation is the one medicine that needs no diagnosis at all, because it treats the underlying condition — the belief in a fixed self and fixed objects — that every one of the fifteen ailments merely expresses in a different guise.

items.en: Concluding in Terms of the Four Siddhāntas

zh: 第四、次明結成悉檀，廣攝佛法者，今約此驗惡根性中辨對治，即以對《摩訶衍論》所明四種悉檀義。所以者何？如十五種不善境界發相，此正是世界悉檀，乃至前明善根發相亦屬世界悉檀，以其皆是因緣生陰入界攝故。次明十五種對治禪門，即是對治悉檀，是中正辨藥病相對故。次明轉治兼轉不轉治，即是為人悉檀。此正逐人根緣不定，方便利益，故名為人。次明非對非轉，即是第一義悉檀，其義可見。故《摩訶衍論》云：「此四悉檀，即攝十二部經八萬四千法藏一切佛法。」理而推之，當知禪門之義，則為廣博，靡所不收。
en: Fourth, next clarifying the conclusion in terms of the siddhāntas, broadly encompassing the Buddhadharma: here, with reference to the antidotes distinguished within this verification of unwholesome capacity, they are now matched against the sense of the four siddhāntas clarified in the Mahāyāna treatise. Why is this? The fifteen kinds of unwholesome states and their marks of arising are precisely the worldly siddhānta — and, further back, the marks of wholesome roots arising already clarified likewise belong to the worldly siddhānta, since both are, in every case, encompassed within the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements arisen through causes and conditions.

Next, the fifteen kinds of antidote-gates of dhyāna just clarified are precisely the siddhānta of the antidote, since it is exactly there that medicine is properly matched against illness. Next, the transposed treatment and the combined transposed-and-non-transposed treatment just clarified are precisely the siddhānta for the individual — this precisely follows each person's own capacity and conditions, unfixed from person to person, benefiting through skillful means according to the individual, hence it is called "for the individual." Next, the treatment that is neither matched nor transposed, just clarified, is precisely the siddhānta of ultimate meaning; its sense can be readily seen.

Hence the Mahāyāna treatise says: "These four siddhāntas encompass the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the eighty-four thousand stores of the Dharma, and the whole of the Buddhadharma." Reasoning this through, one should know that the meaning of the dharma-gates of dhyāna is thus vast and far-reaching, leaving nothing whatsoever outside what it gathers in.

This closing move retroactively reorganizes everything covered since fascicle 3's opening of the second internal-expedient-means layer under Nāgārjuna's four siddhāntas, already introduced back in fascicle 1 topic 5: the wholesome and unwholesome marks themselves as the worldly siddhānta (things simply as they conventionally appear), the fifteen matched antidotes as the siddhānta of the antidote (the specific-remedy level), transposed and combined treatment as the siddhānta for the individual (calibrated to the person, not the abstract diagnosis), and the sixth antidote type — prajñā's right contemplation — as the siddhānta of ultimate meaning. That all four fit so exactly is the treatise's way of showing that this whole elaborate apparatus of fifteen wholesome marks, fifteen unwholesome marks, and six kinds of antidote was never a free-standing system of its own, but a specific application of the same four-siddhānta framework running through the entire treatise. This closes the fourth and final part of verifying unwholesome capacity, the whole of verifying wholesome and unwholesome capacity (明驗善惡根性), and the second of the internal expedient means' five layers.

zh: 第三、次明安心禪門者，略為五意：一、明隨便宜；二、明隨對治成就；三、明隨樂欲；四、明隨次第；五、明隨第一義。
en: Third, next clarifying the dhyāna-gates for settling the mind: in brief, this has five parts — clarifying following what is expedient; clarifying following what the antidote has already accomplished; clarifying following inclination; clarifying following sequence; and clarifying following ultimate meaning.

zh: 今釋第一、隨便宜者，如驗善根性中發十五種禪門，隨其發法，當知過去已經修習，可還修令成就，隨所發法，安心修之，如發覺觸後，欲修安心，當教數息。所以者何？根本初禪多從數息中發，當知是人過去已曾數息修禪。今若從息道而入，與本相扶，禪則易發，加功不止，則能具足四禪空定，因此即發三乘聖道事等。金師之子，教令數息，是為隨本，善根發後，說安心法。餘十四善根發，隨便宜立安心亦如是。
en: Here, the first is now explained: following what is expedient. Among the fifteen dhyāna-gates whose arising was clarified within the arising of wholesome roots, whatever dharma has actually arisen should be understood to have already been cultivated in the past — it can be cultivated again and brought to completion; one should settle the mind by cultivating whatever dharma has actually arisen. For instance, if, after tactile sensations have arisen and been felt, one wishes to settle the mind, one should be taught to count the breath. Why is this? The root first dhyāna, for the most part, arises through counting the breath — hence it should be understood that such a person has already cultivated dhyāna through counting the breath in some past life. If, now, one enters again through the path of the breath, this supports what was already there, and dhyāna is thereby brought forth easily; continuing to apply effort without pause, one is able to become complete in the four dhyānas and the formless concentrations, and, through this, the noble path of the three vehicles and its fruits are brought forth as well.

The goldsmith's son was taught to count the breath — this is precisely following what is already one's own foundation: once the wholesome root has arisen, the method for settling the mind is then given accordingly. The same holds for settling the mind following what is expedient among the remaining fourteen wholesome roots arising as well.

zh: 二、明隨對治成就立安心法者，如行人本有貪欲不善障法，為治此病，作不淨觀，觀成病滅。爾時雖無欲病，而未證深法，當更加心修習不淨。作種種不淨成已，次當却除皮肉，修白骨流光，入八背捨，斷三界結，成三乘道，此則不失其功。若更安心餘法，方復造功，則於事難成。餘十四隨對治成就，辨安心法，類之可知。
en: Second, clarifying settling the mind by following what the antidote has already accomplished: as when a practitioner originally has the unwholesome, obstructing dharma of craving, and, in order to treat this ailment, practices the contemplation of impurity, this contemplation being accomplished and the ailment extinguished. At that point, although the ailment of desire is now absent, deep attainment has not yet been realized — one should apply the mind further still, continuing to cultivate the contemplation of impurity. Having accomplished the various forms of impurity, one should next strip away skin and flesh, cultivating the white bones and their flowing light, entering the eight liberations, severing the fetters of the three realms, and accomplishing the path of the three vehicles — this way, the effort already made is not lost. Were one instead to settle the mind on some other method at this point, effort would have to be built up all over again, and the matter would be difficult to accomplish. The same pattern, settling the mind by following what the antidote has already accomplished, should be understood to hold for the remaining fourteen antidotes as well.

zh: 三、隨樂欲者，若能對治，斷欲界煩惱不善之患，則十五種禪通無遮障。爾時當隨行者心所欲樂諸禪三昧，各安心其門而修習之，即皆開發，始終成就。此可以數人同治修為類。四、約次第立安心法者，遮障既除，自有行人欲從淺至深，具足修一切禪定，應從阿那般那中而教數息；證根本四禪空定已，次教隨息；證十六特勝已，次應觀息；具足通明之禪，次教不淨觀，入九想、背捨等禪，乃至次應觀心性，入九種大禪。禪定次第並如上。第五、明禪次第中，分別修證方法在下自當具說，今明約驗善惡根性，後用安心法。既有如此之便利，故次後而說。
en: Third, following inclination: if one is able, through the antidotes, to sever the afflictive, unwholesome troubles of the desire realm, then all fifteen kinds of dhyāna are open in common, with no obstruction remaining. At that point, one should settle the mind according to whichever dhyāna-samādhi the practitioner's own mind actually delights in and inclines toward, cultivating it through its own gate — and it will be brought forth in every case, accomplished from beginning to end. This may be understood on the model of the Ābhidharma masters' shared treatment through cultivation.

Fourth, establishing the method for settling the mind with reference to sequence: once the obstruction is removed, there are practitioners who wish to proceed from the shallow to the deep, cultivating every dhyāna-concentration in full — such a person should be taught to begin with counting the breath, within mindfulness of the breath; once the four root dhyānas and the formless concentrations are realized, one is next taught to follow the breath; once the sixteen special excellences are realized, one should next observe the breath; once the thorough-and-bright contemplation is complete, one is next taught the contemplation of impurity, entering the nine contemplations, the liberations, and the other such dhyānas; and, further still, one should next contemplate the nature of mind, entering the nine kinds of great dhyāna. The sequence of dhyāna-concentration follows entirely as given above.

The fifth topic's own sequence of dhyāna — its methods of cultivation and realization distinguished in detail — belongs properly below, where it will be given in full; here, it is only clarified with reference to how, once wholesome and unwholesome capacity has been verified, the method for settling the mind is used afterward. Since there is this kind of expedience already available, it is therefore explained here, immediately following.

zh: 五、明隨第一義者，泥洹真法寶，眾生種種門。入此十五種善根發後，及五對治除障已後，隨於一法門易悟之處，即以此為安心者，行人多因是門入聖道也。
en: Fifth, clarifying following ultimate meaning: nirvāṇa, the true jewel of the Dharma — sentient beings enter it through many kinds of gates. After these fifteen kinds of wholesome roots have arisen, and after the obstructions have been removed through the five antidotes, one should settle the mind on whichever single dharma-gate proves easiest to awaken through — practitioners, for the most part, enter the noble path precisely through this gate.

The five ways of settling the mind form a rough sequence of their own: the first two are diagnostic, following whatever the practitioner's own history (past habituation, or the antidote that just worked) has already revealed; the third and fourth are prescriptive, letting the practitioner follow either taste or a fixed curriculum once the obstructions are actually cleared; and the fifth cuts across all of them, settling on whatever single gate — among fifteen wholesome marks and five antidotes now available — happens to be "easiest to awaken through" for this particular person. Read together with fascicle 3's opening pedagogical note (the ideal teacher reads a student's capacity directly; the realistic default is to start everyone with stopping and let the results reveal what comes next), this section is that same diagnostic logic completed: verification tells you what a student has, settling the mind tells you what to do with it.

quiz.q: Where does "combined treatment" come from, and what does the cited passage say?
options: the Mahāyāna treatise on recollecting relinquishment: recognize how many afflictions a being has — one, two mixed, three mixed — and teach that many methods
quiz.why: "This, too, is given in the Mahāyāna treatise, within its explanation of the passage on the eight recollections' recollection of relinquishment ... If there is a single affliction, a single dharma is taught as its treatment; if two are mixed together, two dharmas are taught as their treatment."

quiz.q: Why should one with both craving and anger combine the contemplations of impurity and loving-kindness?
options: one method alone treats one side but aggravates the other; combined, both are cured
quiz.why: "If only a single method were used, although it might treat one side, it would only aggravate the other — this would itself be an error. Here, with the two methods combined together, both ailments are cured at once."

quiz.q: What is the treatment that is neither matched, transposed, nor combined?
options: the right contemplation of prajñā, the siddhānta of ultimate meaning, treating all fifteen ailments and bringing forth all fifteen gates
quiz.why: "Treatment that is neither matched, transposed, nor combined: this is precisely the right contemplation of prajñā, the siddhānta of ultimate meaning. This contemplation is able, in common, to treat all fifteen ailments, and is able, in common, to bring forth all fifteen gates of dhyāna as well."

quiz.q: What Mahāyāna treatise line shows that right contemplation removes all three poisons?
options: apart from the true mark, all is demonic
some samādhis remove only craving, not anger or delusion; some remove all three poisons
to learn all good, learn prajñā
quiz.why: "Hence the Mahāyāna treatise says: 'There is a samādhi able only to remove craving, unable to remove anger or delusion; and there is a samādhi able to remove all three poisons together' — this latter is precisely the right contemplation, the siddhānta of ultimate meaning."

quiz.q: What does the text cite to show right contemplation treats anger?
options: the Prajñāpāramitā: when cut apart by King Kalinga, there was no mark of self, person, or being, so no anger arose
the craving freed by pure contemplation
"how to still chasing? the mind finds nothing"
"when there is brightness there is no darkness"
quiz.why: "Right contemplation is able to treat anger — as the Prajñāpāramitā says: 'When, in the past, I had my body cut apart limb by limb by King Kalinga, at that very moment there was no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being — and so no anger arose.'" The other lines support treating craving, delusion, and discursive thought.

quiz.q: What medicine illustrates the treatment that is neither matched, transposed, nor combined?
options: the agada medicine, which treats every illness
quiz.why: "Every other worldly medicine, each matched to its own particular ailment, able to treat only that one ailment ... The agada medicine, however, is able to treat every ailment universally — this is precisely what is meant by treatment that is neither matched, transposed, nor combined."

quiz.q: To which siddhānta do the fifteen unwholesome states and their marks of arising belong?
options: the worldly siddhānta (so do the wholesome marks, all encompassed in the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements)
quiz.why: "The fifteen kinds of unwholesome states and their marks of arising are precisely the worldly siddhānta — and, further back, the marks of wholesome roots arising already clarified likewise belong to the worldly siddhānta, since both are, in every case, encompassed within the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements arisen through causes and conditions."

quiz.q: To which siddhānta do the fifteen antidote-gates belong, and why?
options: the siddhānta of the antidote, since medicine is matched to illness
quiz.why: "The fifteen kinds of antidote-gates of dhyāna just clarified are precisely the siddhānta of the antidote, since it is exactly there that medicine is properly matched against illness."

quiz.q: Why do transposed and combined treatments belong to the siddhānta for the individual?
options: they follow each person's unfixed capacity and conditions, benefiting through skillful means
quiz.why: "The transposed treatment and the combined transposed-and-non-transposed treatment just clarified are precisely the siddhānta for the individual — this precisely follows each person's own capacity and conditions, unfixed from person to person, benefiting through skillful means."

quiz.q: According to the Mahāyāna treatise, what do the four siddhāntas encompass?
options: the twelve divisions of scripture, the 84,000 Dharma stores, the whole Buddhadharma
quiz.why: "Hence the Mahāyāna treatise says: 'These four siddhāntas encompass the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the eighty-four thousand stores of the Dharma, and the whole of the Buddhadharma.'"

quiz.q: How does right contemplation treat discursive thought, and which sūtra is cited?
options: in right contemplation language and mental activity are cut off, so where could discursive thought arise; Vimalakīrti: "How to still chasing after objects? The mind finds nothing"
quiz.why: "Within right contemplation's own mind, the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished; from what, then, could discursive thought possibly arise? Hence the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: 'How does one bring the chasing after objects to rest? By the mind's having nothing at all that it can find.'"

quiz.q: Settling the mind has five parts. Which?
options: following what is expedient, what the antidote accomplished, inclination, sequence, ultimate meaning
quiz.why: "Clarifying the dhyāna-gates for settling the mind: in brief, this has five parts — clarifying following what is expedient; clarifying following what the antidote has already accomplished; clarifying following inclination; clarifying following sequence; and clarifying following ultimate meaning."

quiz.q: In settling the mind by what is expedient, why teach counting the breath after the tactile sensation arises?
options: the root first dhyāna mostly arises from counting the breath, showing past practice; entering by the breath supports that foundation and dhyāna arises easily
quiz.why: "The root first dhyāna, for the most part, arises through counting the breath — hence it should be understood that such a person has already cultivated dhyāna through counting the breath in some past life. If, now, one enters again through the path of the breath, this supports what was already there, and dhyāna is thereby brought forth easily."

quiz.q: Following what the antidote accomplished: after impurity contemplation has cured craving, what should one do?
options: keep cultivating impurity, strip away skin and flesh to the white bones' flowing light, enter the eight liberations, sever the three realms' fetters — so the effort is not lost
quiz.why: "One should apply the mind further still, continuing to cultivate the contemplation of impurity ... next strip away skin and flesh, cultivating the white bones and their flowing light, entering the eight liberations ... this way, the effort already made is not lost. Were one instead to settle the mind on some other method at this point, effort would have to be built up all over again."

quiz.q: Which order is correct for settling the mind by sequence?
options: counting (root dhyānas and formless) → following (sixteen excellences) → observing (thorough-and-bright) → impurity → contemplating mind (nine great dhyānas)
quiz.why: "Such a person should be taught to begin with counting the breath ... once the four root dhyānas and the formless concentrations are realized, one is next taught to follow the breath; once the sixteen special excellences are realized, one should next observe the breath; once the thorough-and-bright contemplation is complete, one is next taught the contemplation of impurity ... and, further still, one should next contemplate the nature of mind, entering the nine kinds of great dhyāna."
